claim: Amyloid β (Aβ) forms aggregates in the Alzheimer's disease brain.
source: Amyloid β (Aβ) forms aggregates in the Alzheimer's disease brain and is well known for its pathological roles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in Alzheimer's disease research, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Aβ regulates neuronal physiology in the healthy brain.
source: Recent studies show that it also regulates neuronal physiology in the healthy brain.
evidence: The claim references recent studies, indicating citation-based support.

claim: A novel signaling pathway activated by monomeric Aβ plays essential roles in regulating microglial activity during mouse development.
source: In this article, we describe the discovery of a novel signaling pathway activated by the monomeric form of Aβ in vitro that plays essential roles in the regulation of microglial activity and the assembly of neocortex during mouse development in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Activation of the monomeric Aβ pathway depends on the function of amyloid precursor protein (APP) and Ric8a in microglia.
source: We find that activation of this pathway depends on the function of amyloid precursor and the heterotrimeric G protein regulator Ric8a in microglia and inhibits microglial immune activation at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from genetic mutant analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The monomeric Aβ pathway inhibits microglial immune activation at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
source: We find that activation of this pathway depends on the function of amyloid precursor and the heterotrimeric G protein regulator Ric8a in microglia and inhibits microglial immune activation at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cytokine secretion and mRNA expression changes.

claim: Genetic disruption of the monomeric Aβ pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation.
source: Genetic disruption of this pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation and excessive matrix proteinase activation, leading to basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from genetic mutant analyses.

claim: Genetic disruption of the monomeric Aβ pathway leads to excessive matrix proteinase activation.
source: Genetic disruption of this pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation and excessive matrix proteinase activation, leading to basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased MMP9 activity in mutants.

claim: Genetic disruption of the monomeric Aβ pathway leads to basement membrane degradation.
source: Genetic disruption of this pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation and excessive matrix proteinase activation, leading to basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing laminin staining defects in mutants.

claim: Genetic disruption of the monomeric Aβ pathway leads to neuronal ectopia.
source: Genetic disruption of this pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation and excessive matrix proteinase activation, leading to basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ectopia formation in mutants.

claim: Genetic disruption of the monomeric Aβ pathway leads to laminar disruption.
source: Genetic disruption of this pathway during neocortical development results in microglial dysregulation and excessive matrix proteinase activation, leading to basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cortical organization defects in mutants.

claim: Aβ functions as a negative regulator of brain microglia.
source: These results uncover a previously unknown function of Aβ as a negative regulator of brain microglia and substantially elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Aβ monomers suppress microglial cytokine expression.

claim: Aβ monomer depletion may play a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Considering the prominence of Aβ and neuroinflammation in the pathology of Alzheimer's disease, they also highlight a potentially overlooked role of Aβ monomer depletion in the development of the disease.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Aβ oligomers are highly toxic.
source: Studies have shown that the oligomers formed by Aβ are highly toxic, with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of multiple forms of synaptic plasticity (Gulisano et al., 2018; He et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013; Laurén et al., 2009; Lazarevic et al., 2017; Parodi et al., 2010; Puzzo et al., 2008; Shankar et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ oligomers inhibit neurotransmitter release.
source: Studies have shown that the oligomers formed by Aβ are highly toxic, with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of multiple forms of synaptic plasticity (Gulisano et al., 2018; He et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013; Laurén et al., 2009; Lazarevic et al., 2017; Parodi et al., 2010; Puzzo et al., 2008; Shankar et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ oligomers deplete synaptic vesicle pools.
source: Studies have shown that the oligomers formed by Aβ are highly toxic, with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of multiple forms of synaptic plasticity (Gulisano et al., 2018; He et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013; Laurén et al., 2009; Lazarevic et al., 2017; Parodi et al., 2010; Puzzo et al., 2008; Shankar et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ oligomers disrupt postsynaptic organization and function.
source: Studies have shown that the oligomers formed by Aβ are highly toxic, with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of multiple forms of synaptic plasticity (Gulisano et al., 2018; He et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013; Laurén et al., 2009; Lazarevic et al., 2017; Parodi et al., 2010; Puzzo et al., 2008; Shankar et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ oligomers impair multiple forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: Studies have shown that the oligomers formed by Aβ are highly toxic, with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of multiple forms of synaptic plasticity (Gulisano et al., 2018; He et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013; Laurén et al., 2009; Lazarevic et al., 2017; Parodi et al., 2010; Puzzo et al., 2008; Shankar et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The toxic effects of Aβ oligomers significantly underpin the pathogenic role of Aβ in Alzheimer's disease.
source: These effects likely significantly underpin the pathogenic role of Aβ in Alzheimer's disease and contribute to neuron loss and cognitive decline in patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited toxic effects of Aβ oligomers.

claim: Aβ is produced in the healthy brain by neurons in a neural activity-dependent manner.
source: Besides its pathological roles, recent studies show that Aβ is also produced in the healthy brain by neurons in a neural activity-dependent manner and regulates the normal physiology of neurons (Cirrito et al., 2005; Fogel et al., 2014; Galanis et al., 2021; Garcia-Osta and Alberini, 2009; Gulisano et al., 2018; Gulisano et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2010; Palmeri et al., 2017; Puzzo et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ monomers and low-molecular-weight oligomers positively regulate synaptic function and plasticity.
source: For example, consistent with studies showing that Aβ monomers and low-molecular-weight oligomers positively regulate synaptic function and plasticity, administration of these molecules in vivo has been found to improve learning and memory in animals (Fogel et al., 2014; Garcia-Osta and Alberini, 2009; Gulisano et al., 2018; Gulisano et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2010; Palmeri et al., 2017; Puzzo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Administration of Aβ monomers and low-molecular-weight oligomers in vivo improves learning and memory in animals.
source: For example, consistent with studies showing that Aβ monomers and low-molecular-weight oligomers positively regulate synaptic function and plasticity, administration of these molecules in vivo has been found to improve learning and memory in animals (Fogel et al., 2014; Garcia-Osta and Alberini, 2009; Gulisano et al., 2018; Gulisano et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2010; Palmeri et al., 2017; Puzzo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ monomers directly promote synapse formation and function.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have shown that Aβ monomers directly promote synapse formation and function and homeostatic plasticity, processes crucial to normal cognitive function (Galanis et al., 2021; Kamenetz et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ monomers promote homeostatic plasticity.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have shown that Aβ monomers directly promote synapse formation and function and homeostatic plasticity, processes crucial to normal cognitive function (Galanis et al., 2021; Kamenetz et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia and astrocytes play critical roles in the normal development, function, and plasticity of the brain circuitry.
source: Microglia and astrocytes, two of the major glial cell types in the brain, are known to play critical roles in the normal development, function, and plasticity of the brain circuitry (Barres, 2008; Schafer and Stevens, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia and astrocytes coordinately regulate the spatiotemporally specific expression of immune cytokines in the brain.
source: They coordinately regulate, among others, the spatiotemporally specific expression of immune cytokines in the brain that regulate numerous processes of brain circuit development, function, and plasticity (Zipp et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the thalamus, populations of astrocytes activate the expression of interleukin-33 in a neural activity-dependent manner.
source: For example, in the thalamus, a key relay station in the visual pathway, populations of astrocytes have been found to activate the expression of interleukin-33 in a neural activity-dependent manner, induce activity-dependent elimination of supernumerary synapses, and promote the maturation of the visual circuitry in early postnatal life (Vainchtein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the thalamus, astrocytes induce activity-dependent elimination of supernumerary synapses.
source: For example, in the thalamus, a key relay station in the visual pathway, populations of astrocytes have been found to activate the expression of interleukin-33 in a neural activity-dependent manner, induce activity-dependent elimination of supernumerary synapses, and promote the maturation of the visual circuitry in early postnatal life (Vainchtein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the adult hippocampus, astrocytes activate the expression of interleukin-33 under neuronal activity blockade.
source: In the adult hippocampus, in contrast, astrocytes have been found to activate the expression of interleukin-33 under neuronal activity blockade and induce homeostatic synaptic plasticity that maintains circuit activity balance (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the striatum and neocortex, astrocytes and microglia activate the expression of TNFα upon changes in neural circuit activity.
source: In the striatum and the neocortex, not only have astrocytes but also have microglia been observed to activate the expression of TNFα (Tumor Necrosis Factor α) upon changes in neural circuit activity and induce homeostatic synaptic plasticity that dampens circuit perturbation (Heir et al., 2024; Lewitus et al., 2016; Stellwagen and Malenka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglial release of cytokines such as TNFα underpins the application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation.
source: In the clinic, the induction of microglial release of cytokines such as TNFα also underpins the application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, a noninvasive brain stimulation technique frequently used to induce cortical plasticity and treat pharmaco-resistant depression (Eichler et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Glial activation and brain cytokine elevation are key pathologic factors in Alzheimer's disease development.
source: In neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, glial activation, and brain cytokine elevation are also key pathologic factors in disease development (Colonna and Butovsky, 2017; Patani et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Elevated TNFα expression by microglia underlies interneuron deficits and autism-like phenotype linked to maternal immune activation.
source: Furthermore, elevated TNFα expression by microglia also underlies interneuron deficits and autism-like phenotype linked to maternal immune activation (Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of Ric8a using Emx1-Cre results in ectopia formation exclusively in the lateral cortex of the perinatal mutant brain.
source: We found it result in ectopia formation exclusively in the lateral cortex of the perinatal mutant brain (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants consisted of both early- and late-born neurons.
source: Birth-dating showed that the ectopia consisted of both early- and late-born neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons in the ectopia stained positive for both Ctip2 and Cux1.
source: Consistent with this observation, neurons in the ectopia also stained positive for both Ctip2 and Cux1, genes specific to lower- and upper-layer neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: In cortical areas without ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, radial migration of early- and late-born neurons appeared largely normal.
source: Interestingly, in cortical areas without ectopia, radial migration of early- and late-born neurons appeared largely normal as shown by birth-dating as well as Cux1 and Ctip2 staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell-autonomous defects in neurons are unlikely the cause of the ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: This suggests that cell-autonomous defects in neurons are unlikely the cause of the ectopia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that neuronal migration appears normal in areas without ectopia.

claim: At E16.5, clear breaches in the pial basement membrane of the developing cortex were apparent in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: At E16.5, clear breaches in the pial basement membrane of the developing cortex were already apparent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Radial glial fibers in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants extended beyond the breaches in the basement membrane.
source: However, unlike classic models of cobblestone lissencephaly, where radial glial fibers typically retract, radial glial fibers in ric8a mutants instead extended beyond the breaches.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: Radial glial cell adhesion defects are unlikely the cause of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: This argues against radial glial cell adhesion defects since they would be predicted to retract.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that radial glial fibers extend beyond breaches rather than retract.

claim: In areas without ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells was observed.
source: Furthermore, in areas without ectopia, we also observed normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells, expression of Reelin, and splitting of the preplate, arguing against primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: Primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells are unlikely the cause of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Furthermore, in areas without ectopia, we also observed normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells, expression of Reelin, and splitting of the preplate, arguing against primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of normal Cajal–Retzius cell localization and function.

claim: In Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, large numbers of basement membrane breaches were observed at E14.5, almost all associated with ectopia.
source: In Ric8a mutants, we observed large numbers of basement membrane breaches at E14.5, almost all associated with ectopia (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: At E13.5 in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, significant numbers of basement membrane breaches were observed, but none was associated with ectopia.
source: In contrast, at E13.5, although we also observed significant numbers of breaches, none was associated with ectopia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: Basement membrane breaches precede ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: This indicates that basement membrane breaches similarly precede ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of breaches and ectopia formation.

claim: At E12.5 in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, increased numbers of laminin-positive debris were observed across the lateral cortex.
source: However, at E12.5, despite a complete lack of basement membrane breaches, we observed increased numbers of laminin-positive debris across the lateral cortex, both beneath basement membrane segments with intact laminin staining and beneath segments with disrupted laminin staining, the latter presumably sites of future breach (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Excessive basement membrane degradation is likely a primary cause of cortical ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Thus, these results indicate that excessive basement membrane degradation, but not defective maintenance, is likely a primary cause of cortical ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased laminin debris preceding breaches and ectopia.

claim: Deletion of Ric8a by Nestin-Cre did not result in ectopia.
source: To our surprise, deletion of Ric8a by Nestin-Cre did not result in ectopia (Ma et al., 2017; Figure 1g, g').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and cited previous study.

claim: Combined deletion of Ric8a from neural progenitors, post-mitotic neurons, and astrocytes does not lead to ectopia.
source: Since Nestin-Cre-mediated deletion in neural progenitors is inherited by post-mitotic neurons and astrocytes, this indicates that the combined deletion of Ric8a from all these cell types does not lead to ectopia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ectopia in Nestin-Cre mutants.

claim: Ric8a deletion using Foxg1-Cre failed to produce ectopia.
source: We found that Ric8a deletion using Foxg1-Cre still failed to produce ectopia (Figure 1h, h').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is not responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
source: Thus, these results strongly argue against the interpretation that Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ectopia when Ric8a is deleted using various neural-specific Cre lines.

claim: Brain microglia express Emx1 at a significant level.
source: To assess the role of non-neural cell types, we turned our attention to microglia since RNA-seq studies show that brain microglia express Emx1 at a significant level (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous RNA-seq study.

claim: Emx1-Cre-mediated Ric8a deletion resulted in altered cytokine expression in microglia.
source: We found that Emx1-Cre-mediated Ric8a deletion resulted in altered cytokine expression in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia.
source: This indicate that Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia and deletes Ric8a.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of altered cytokine expression in microglia from Emx1-Cre mutants.

claim: When crossed to a reporter, Emx1-Cre resulted in the expression of reporter gene in microglia.
source: In further support of this interpretation, we found that when crossed to a reporter, Emx1-Cre resulted in the expression of reporter gene in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–c'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Emx1-Cre resulted in the reduction of Ric8a mRNA levels in microglia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: It also resulted in the reduction of Ric8a mRNA levels in in microglia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine secretion in comparison to control microglia upon LPS stimulation.
source: Like Emx1-Cre mutants, Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia also showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription in comparison to control microglia upon stimulation by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine transcription in comparison to control microglia upon LPS stimulation.
source: Like Emx1-Cre mutants, Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia also showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription in comparison to control microglia upon stimulation by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription upon stimulation by poly I:C.
source: Similar results were also obtained with stimulation by polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly I:C), an intracellular immune activator.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA and qRT-PCR assays.

claim: Ric8a deficiency in microglia results in broad increases in microglial sensitivity to immune stimulation.
source: Thus, these results indicate that ric8a deficiency in microglia results in broad increases in microglial sensitivity to immune stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated cytokine responses to multiple immune stimuli.

claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants did not show ectopia without LPS treatment.
source: To determine if microglial Ric8a deficiency alone is sufficient to cause cortical ectopia in vivo, we examined Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants but found that it did not affect either basement membrane integrity or cortical layering (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Over 50% of Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5.
source: We found that over 50% of Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5 (10 of 19 mutant neonates examined) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No cortical ectopia were observed in any of the 32 littermate controls that were administered LPS.
source: In contrast, no cortical ectopia were observed in any of the 32 littermate controls that were similarly administered LPS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis.

claim: Only the combination of microglial Ric8a deficiency and immune activation leads to ectopia formation.
source: This indicates that only the combination of microglial Ric8a deficiency and immune activation leads to ectopia formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia only form when both conditions are present.

claim: Ric8a deletion by the dual Cre combination of Cx3cr1-Cre and Nestin-Cre resulted in severe ectopia in all double Cre mutants.
source: However, we found that, like deletion by Emx1-Cre, ric8a deletion by the dual Cre combination of Cx3cr1-Cre and Nestin-Cre also resulted in severe ectopia in all double Cre mutants (six of six examined) (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Elevated immune activation of Ric8a deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.
source: Thus, these results indicate that elevated immune activation of Ric8a deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia form when Ric8a-deficient microglia are activated.

claim: The Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant is unique in that ectopia are not observed at the cortical midline but are instead exclusively located to the lateral cortex.
source: There are only a few mutants including the Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant that are exception, in that the ectopia are not observed at the cortical midline but are instead exclusively located to the lateral cortex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The other mutants with ectopia exclusively in the lateral cortex include the App/Aplp1/2 triple and Apbb1/2 double knockouts.
source: The other mutants in this unique group include the App/Aplp1/2 triple (Herms et al., 2004) and Apbb1/2 double knockouts (Guénette et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Similar mechanisms involving microglia may underlie ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre, App/Aplp1/2, and Apbb1/2 mutants.
source: This suggests that similar mechanisms involving microglia may underlie ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre, App/Aplp1/2, and Apbb1/2 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of ectopia phenotypes.

claim: Specific App knockdown in cortical neurons during development results in under-migration of targeted neurons.
source: For example, unlike the triple knockout, which causes neuronal over-migration, specific App knockdown in cortical neurons during development results in under- instead of over-migration of targeted neurons (Young-Pearse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species.
source: Furthermore, Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and we confirmed that Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices.
source: Furthermore, Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and we confirmed that Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microglia cultured from App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants showed reduced TNFα and IL-6 secretion upon stimulation.
source: To this end, we employed Cx3cr1-Cre to delete a conditional allele of App from microglia and found that microglia cultured from App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants showed reduced TNFα and IL-6 secretion as well as muted IL-6 transcription upon stimulation (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: App plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia in regulating microglial activity.
source: This indicates that App plays a previously unrecognized, cell-autonomous role in microglia in regulating microglial activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of altered cytokine responses in App mutant microglia.

claim: App mutant peritoneal macrophages showed significantly elevated secretion of all cytokines tested upon LPS stimulation.
source: We found that App mutant macrophages showed significantly elevated secretion of all cytokines tested (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: App mutant peritoneal macrophages showed increased mRNA induction for all cytokines tested upon LPS stimulation.
source: At the transcriptional level, mRNA induction was also increased for all cytokines (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The normal function of App is to suppress the inflammatory activation of microglia.
source: Thus, like that of Ric8a, the normal function of App also appears to be to suppress the inflammatory activation of microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated cytokine responses in App mutant microglia and macrophages.

claim: A significant number of App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5.
source: We found that, while none of the 81 littermate controls administered LPS showed ectopia, a significant number of mutant neonates showed ectopia (6 of 31 neonates examined, ~19%) and associated breaches in the basement membrane (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: App-deficient microglia, when activated, results in cortical ectopia during development.
source: Thus, app deficient microglia, when activated, also results in cortical ectopia during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia form in App mutants when microglia are activated by LPS.

claim: App normally plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia that negatively regulates microglial activation.
source: Thus, these results indicate that App normally plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia that negatively regulate microglial activation, and its loss of function underlies cortical ectopia formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that App-deficient microglia show elevated activation and cause ectopia when stimulated.

claim: App and Ric8a form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.
source: The similarities between App and Ric8a mutant phenotypes suggest that they form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes between App and Ric8a mutants.

claim: Aβ has nanomolar direct binding affinity to APP.
source: Several molecules have been reported to bind to APP and/or activate APP-dependent pathways (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2012), among which Aβ is noteworthy for its nanomolar direct binding affinity (Fogel et al., 2014; Shaked et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ oligomers and fibrils are pro-inflammatory.
source: Aβ oligomers and fibrils have been shown by numerous studies to be pro-inflammatory, while non-fibrillar Aβ lack such activity (Halle et al., 2008; Huang, 2023; Huang, 2024; Lorton et al., 1996; Muehlhauser et al., 2001; Tan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Non-fibrillar Aβ lack pro-inflammatory activity.
source: Aβ oligomers and fibrils have been shown by numerous studies to be pro-inflammatory, while non-fibrillar Aβ lack such activity (Halle et al., 2008; Huang, 2023; Huang, 2024; Lorton et al., 1996; Muehlhauser et al., 2001; Tan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ inhibits T cell activation when employed under conditions that favor the monomer conformation.
source: In contrast, when employed under conditions that favor the monomer conformation, Aβ inhibits T cell activation (Grant et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aβ monomers potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines by microglia.
source: We found that Aβ monomers as prepared potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed similar effects on microglia no matter if they were activated by LPS or poly I:C (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aβ monomers showed similar suppressive effects on microglia whether they were activated by LPS or poly I:C.
source: We found that Aβ monomers as prepared potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed similar effects on microglia no matter if they were activated by LPS or poly I:C (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Aβ monomers strongly inhibited the induction of cytokines at the transcriptional level.
source: We also found that the Aβ monomers similarly strongly inhibited the induction of cytokines at the transcriptional level (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Monomeric Aβ possesses a previously unreported anti-inflammatory activity against microglia.
source: Thus, these results indicate that monomeric Aβ possesses a previously unreported anti-inflammatory activity against microglia that strongly inhibits microglial inflammatory activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers suppress cytokine expression by microglia.

claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of all tested cytokines by App mutant microglia.
source: We found that, unlike that of control microglia, Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of all tested cytokines by App mutant microglia (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aβ monomers still significantly suppressed cytokine secretion by Aplp2 mutant microglia.
source: Interestingly, this blockade appeared to be specific to App since Aβ monomers still significantly suppressed cytokine secretion by Aplp2 mutant microglia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA assays.

claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress cytokine induction in App mutant microglia at the transcriptional level.
source: At the transcriptional level, Aβ monomers also failed to suppress cytokine induction in App mutant microglia (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: APP is functionally required in microglia for Aβ monomer inhibition of cytokine expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
source: Together, these results indicate that APP is functionally required in microglia for Aβ monomer inhibition of cytokine expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers fail to suppress cytokine expression in App mutant microglia.

claim: Cytokine secretion by control macrophages was strongly suppressed by Aβ monomers.
source: We found that, like that of control microglia, cytokine secretion by control macrophages was also strongly suppressed by Aβ monomers (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: App mutant macrophages failed to respond to Aβ monomers.
source: However, even though App mutant macrophages showed elevated response to immune stimulation in comparison to control macrophages, they still failed to respond to Aβ monomers and displayed levels of cytokine secretion that were indistinguishable from those of DMSO-treated cells (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: APP function is required in microglia for mediating the anti-inflammatory effects of Aβ monomers.
source: Thus, these results further indicate that APP function is required in microglia for mediating the anti-inflammatory effects of Aβ monomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that App mutant macrophages fail to respond to Aβ monomers.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and in vivo.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and vivo (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and that Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins (Gabay et al., 2011; Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and vivo (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and that Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins (Gabay et al., 2011; Tall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of TNFα and IL-6 by Ric8a mutant microglia.
source: We found that, indeed, like that of App mutant microglia, Aβ monomers also failed to suppress the secretion of TNFα and IL-6 by Ric8a mutant microglia (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Heterotrimeric G protein function is likely required in the same pathway as APP in microglia for the suppression of TNFα and IL-6 secretion.
source: This indicates that heterotrimeric G proteins function is likely required in the same pathway of APP in microglia for the suppression of TNFα and IL-6 secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers fail to suppress TNFα and IL-6 secretion in Ric8a mutant microglia.

claim: Aβ monomers still suppressed IL-1β secretion by Ric8a mutant microglia.
source: However, unlike APP, we found that Ric8a appears to be dispensable for Aβ monomer regulation of other cytokines. For example, unlike that of TNFα and IL-6, Aβ monomers still suppressed IL-1β secretion by Ric8a mutant microglia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ric8a is dispensable for Aβ monomer regulation of cytokine transcription.
source: It also appears to be dispensable for the regulation of cytokine transcription since Aβ monomers similarly suppressed IL-6 transcriptional induction in both control and Ric8a mutant microglia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR assays.

claim: Heterotrimeric G protein function may only mediate some of the anti-inflammatory signaling of monomeric Aβ.
source: These results suggest that heterotrimeric G proteins function may only mediate some of the anti-inflammatory signaling of monomeric Aβ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ric8a is dispensable for some but not all Aβ monomer effects.

claim: APP and Ric8a-regulated heterotrimeric G proteins form part of a novel anti-inflammatory pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in microglia.
source: Thus, APP and Ric8a-regulated heterotrimeric G proteins form part of a novel anti-inflammatory pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both APP and Ric8a are required for some Aβ monomer effects.

claim: Dorsomorphin and S3I-201 suppressed astrogliosis associated with neuroinflammation in the cortex of Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Consistent with their anti-inflammatory activity, we found that dorsomorphin and S3I-201 both suppressed astrogliosis associated with neuroinflammation in the cortex of Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dorsomorphin and S3I-201 suppressed the formation of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Furthermore, they also suppressed the formation of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, reducing both the number and the size of the ectopia observed (Figure 5a–f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The combined administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 nearly eliminated all ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Most strikingly, the combined administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 nearly eliminated all ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5d, e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation in Ric8a mutants.
source: Thus, these results indicate that excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation in ric8a mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that anti-inflammatory drugs suppress ectopia formation.

claim: At E13.5, MMP9 mRNA is strongly expressed in a sparse cell population resembling microglia populating the cortex.
source: We found that at E13.5, MMP9 mRNA is strongly expressed in a sparse cell population resembling microglia populating the cortex at this stage (Squarzoni et al., 2014; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claim: The activity of MMP9 in the mutant cortex was significantly increased.
source: We found that the activity of MMP9 in the mutant cortex was significantly increased (Figure 5i, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The activity of MMP2 remained unaffected in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: In contrast, that activity of MMP2 remained unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gel zymography.

claim: The immunoreactivity for MMP9 was increased in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
source: Similarly, at the protein level, we found that the immunoreactivity for MMP9 was increased in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5g, h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: BB94 administration significantly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
source: We found that BB94 administration significantly suppress both the number and the size of the ectopia in ric8a mutants (Figure 5j–m).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MMP-9/MMP-13 inhibitor I significantly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
source: To narrow down the identity of MMPs responsible, we further employed an inhibitor specific for MMP9 and 13 (MMP-9/MMP-13 inhibitor I, CAS 204140-01-2) and found that it similarly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia (Figure 5l, m).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Co-administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 reduced MMP9 activity in the mutant cortex to the control level.
source: Furthermore, consistent with its near complete suppression of cortical ectopia (Figure 5a–f), we found that the co-administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 also reduced MMP9 activity in the mutant cortex to the control level (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Aβ monomer-regulated anti-inflammatory pathway normally promotes cortical development through suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
source: Thus, these results indicate this Aβ monomer-regulated anti-inflammatory pathway normally promotes cortical development through suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that inhibiting microglial activation or MMP activity suppresses ectopia formation.

claim: Microglial activity has been found to regulate the size of the cortical neural precursor pool.
source: Indeed, microglial activity has been found to regulate the size of the cortical neural precursor pool (Cunningham et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Microglia-secreted cytokines have been found to promote both neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis.
source: Microglia-secreted cytokines have also been found to promote both neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis (Shigemoto-Mogami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Reductions in the expression of microglial immune and chemotaxis genes lead to the failure of microglia to populate the brain.
source: Previous studies have shown that reductions in the expression of microglial immune and chemotaxis genes instead lead to the failure of microglia to populate the brain (Iyer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins directly interact with the APP cytoplasmic domain.
source: This is also consistent with previous studies showing that heterotrimeric G proteins directly interact with the APP cytoplasmic domain and mediate key branches of APP signaling from invertebrates to mammals (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pancortin, a member of the olfactomedin family proteins, is expressed in the cortex at early developmental stages.
source: However, studies have shown that other APP ligands such as pancortin, a member of the olfactomedin family proteins known to inhibit innate immunity (Liu et al., 2010), are expressed in the cortex at this stage (Rice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pancortin is known to inhibit innate immunity.
source: However, studies have shown that other APP ligands such as pancortin, a member of the olfactomedin family proteins known to inhibit innate immunity (Liu et al., 2010), are expressed in the cortex at this stage (Rice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of Nestin-Cre is influenced by several factors including transgene insertion site and genetic background.
source: The expression of Nestin-Cre, however, is known to be influenced by several factors including transgene insertion site and genetic background and the same Nestin-Cre has been reported to be active and induce gene inactivation in microglia (Karasinska et al., 2013; Takamori et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nestin-Cre has been reported to be active and induce gene inactivation in microglia.
source: The expression of Nestin-Cre, however, is known to be influenced by several factors including transgene insertion site and genetic background and the same Nestin-Cre has been reported to be active and induce gene inactivation in microglia (Karasinska et al., 2013; Takamori et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ is primarily produced by neurons in the brain in a neural activity-dependent manner.
source: Aβ is primarily produced by neurons in the brain in a neural activity-dependent manner and form oligomers when large quantities are produced (Cirrito et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aβ forms oligomers when large quantities are produced.
source: Aβ is primarily produced by neurons in the brain in a neural activity-dependent manner and form oligomers when large quantities are produced (Cirrito et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aβ oligomers increase glial cytokine expression.
source: Aβ oligomers, in contrary to monomers, are pro-inflammatory and increase glial cytokine expression (Halle et al., 2008; Huang, 2023; Lorton et al., 1996; Muehlhauser et al., 2001; Tan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Following sensory deprivation, Aβ levels may be lowered due to loss of sensory stimulation.
source: Following sensory deprivation, for example, Aβ levels may be lowered due to loss of sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known activity-dependent production of Aβ.

claim: Lowered Aβ levels may lead to the relief of monomeric Aβ inhibition of cytokines such as TNFα and trigger homeostatic upscaling of cortical synapses in the visual cortex.
source: This may lead to the relief of monomeric Aβ inhibition of cytokines such as TNFα and as a result trigger homeostatic upscaling of cortical synapses in the visual cortex (Barnes et al., 2017; Heir et al., 2024; Kaneko et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study and cited previous studies.

claim: When neural activity levels are high, large quantities of Aβ may be produced, leading to formation of Aβ oligomers that may induce expression of cytokines such as IL-33 that promote synaptic pruning.
source: In contrary, when neural activity levels are high, large quantities of Aβ may be produced, leading to formation of Aβ oligomers that may in turn induce expression of cytokines such as IL-33 that promote synaptic pruning.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Aβ and related pathways mediate homeostatic and competitive plasticity in the visual and other systems of the brain.
source: A large body of evidence strongly indicates that Aβ and related pathways indeed mediate homeostatic and competitive plasticity in the visual and other systems of the brain (Galanis et al., 2021; Huang, 2023; Huang, 2024; Kamenetz et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the visual cortex, MMP9 is a pivotal mediator of TNFα-dependent homeostatic upscaling of central synapses following monocular deprivation.
source: Indeed, independent studies have shown that, in the visual cortex, MMP9 is also a pivotal mediator of TNFα-dependent homeostatic upscaling of central synapses following monocular deprivation (Akol et al., 2022; Kaneko et al., 2008; Kelly et al., 2015; Spolidoro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the Xenopus tectum, MMP9 has been found to be induced by neural activity and promote visual activity-induced dendritic growth.
source: In the Xenopus tectum, MMP9 has similarly been found to be induced by neural activity and promote visual activity-induced dendritic growth (Gore et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In both wildtype and amblyopic animals, light reintroduction after dark exposure has been found to reactivate plasticity in the adult visual cortex via MMP9.
source: Importantly, in both wildtype and amblyopic animals, light reintroduction after dark exposure has been found to reactivate plasticity in the adult visual cortex via MMP9, uncovering a potential treatment for common visual conditions (Murase et al., 2017; Murase et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In ocular dominance plasticity, MMP9 is activated at perisynaptic regions.
source: In ocular dominance plasticity, MMP9 is activated at perisynaptic regions (Murase et al., 2017; Murase et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MMP9 mRNA translation has been observed in dendrites.
source: MMP9 mRNA translation has been also observed in dendrites (Dziembowska et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Aβ monomers are directly protective to neurons.
source: It is in alignment with recent studies showing that Aβ monomers are also directly protective to neurons and positively regulate synapse development and function (Galanis et al., 2021; Giuffrida et al., 2009; Plant et al., 2003; Ramsden et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aβ monomers positively regulate synapse development and function.
source: It is in alignment with recent studies showing that Aβ monomers are also directly protective to neurons and positively regulate synapse development and function (Galanis et al., 2021; Giuffrida et al., 2009; Plant et al., 2003; Ramsden et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The formation of Aβ oligomers and aggregates in the brain would be predicted to result in the depletion of Aβ monomers.
source: Assuming a set amount of Aβ peptides, the formation of Aβ oligomers and aggregates in the brain would, by chemical law, be predicted to result in the depletion of Aβ monomers (Dear et al., 2020; Michaels et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on chemical principles and supported by citations.

claim: In the Alzheimer's disease brain, there may be a depletion of Aβ monomers taking place that may contribute to the development of neuroinflammation and neuronal damage.
source: Thus, in the Alzheimer's disease brain, besides the obvious formation of Aβ aggregates, there may also be a less visible depletion of Aβ monomers taking place at the same time, which may, like Aβ oligomers, also contribute to the development of neuroinflammation and neuronal damage (Huang, 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study and a citation.

claim: High soluble brain Aβ42 has been found to preserve cognition in patients of both familial and sporadic Alzheimer's disease, in spite of increasing amyloidosis.
source: In support of this interpretation, high soluble brain Aβ42, which likely also means high levels of Aβ monomers in the brain, have been found in clinical studies to preserve cognition in patients of both familial and sporadic Alzheimer's disease, in spite of increasing amyloidosis detected in their brains (Espay et al., 2021; Sturchio et al., 2022; Sturchio et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: In neurodegenerative diseases, MMP9 has been found to be a key determinant regulating the selective degeneration of neuronal cell types.
source: Importantly, in neurodegenerative diseases, MMP9 has been similarly found to be a key determinant regulating the selective degeneration of neuronal cell types (Kaplan et al., 2014; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MMP9 levels are upregulated in the plasma in both mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease patients.
source: MMP9 levels are also upregulated in the plasma in both mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease patients (Bruno et al., 2009; Lorenzl et al., 2008; Tsiknia et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In several motor neuron disease models, reducing MMP9 has been found to protect neurons and delay the loss of motor function.
source: In addition, in several motor neuron disease models, reducing MMP9 has been found to protect neurons and delay the loss of motor function (Kaplan et al., 2014; Spiller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
